Okay, so every coding interview eventually hits you with the same question: what's the Big O of this? And honestly, you can read it right off the code. Let me show you.
Big O isn't about seconds, or how fast your laptop is. It's really just one question. If the input doubles... what happens to the work?
Let's start with the easy one. O of one. A hash lookup just jumps straight to the answer. Ten items, ten million, doesn't matter. It's pretty much one step.
Next up, O of n. That's a single loop, touching each item once. So if you double the input... yep, you double the work.

And here's the one that gets people. O of n squared. It's a loop inside a loop, so every item gets checked against every other item. Eight numbers? Twenty-eight checks. A million numbers? We're talking about five hundred BILLION.
So when n doubles: O of one stays the same. O of n doubles. And O of n squared? Four times the work. We actually timed it, and yeah, that's exactly what happened.
So next time you spot a loop inside a loop in an interview, call it out. That's O of n squared. Then aim for O of n, usually with a hash map. Save this one, and learn the rest on leet Expert.
